title: The Man Who Survived an Iron Rod Through His Skull
sources: Phineas Gage, a railroad construction foreman in Cavendish, Vermont, was injured on 13 September 1848 while blasting rock for the Rutland and Burlington Railroad (Harlow 1848, 1868; Macmillan, 'An Odd Kind of Fame', 2000)
The tamping iron was 3 feet 7 inches (about 1.1 m) long, 1.25 inches across, and weighed 13.25 lb (about 6 kg) (Harlow 1868; Warren Anatomical Museum)
It entered under his left cheekbone, passed behind the left eye, and exited through the top of the skull; it landed some 25 m (about 80 feet) away (Harlow 1868; Van Horn et al. 2012, PLoS ONE)
Gage was conscious and speaking within minutes of the accident (Harlow 1848)
The iron destroyed much of his left frontal lobe; friends said he was 'no longer Gage' (Harlow 1868; Damasio et al. 1994, Science)
He lived about 12 more years, dying in 1860; his skull and the tamping iron are on display at Harvard's Warren Anatomical Museum
